solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Grip metal joint with reversible faces (8)

indicators.note: A word's face is its front, so two words whose faces are reversible can swap their opening letters.

blocks.note: Lead is a metal; it hands its L to the other word and takes the H.
The hock is the ankle joint of a horse's hind leg; it swaps its H for the L.

annotation.walkthrough: The swap here is done by letters rather than sounds, so it reads like a Spooner exchange even though the vowels never change.
annotation.surface: A plumber's instruction for gripping a metal fitting whose faces can be turned either way.
annotation.definitionFit: A wrestler's grip locking the arm round an opponent's head is exactly what the answer names.

entries.clue: Dope accompanying a large female on a cycle (7)

indicators.note: Letters on a cycle go round like a wheel, so the one at the back comes round to the front.

blocks.note: Kept as it is.
L = large, as on clothing labels.
F = female.
With = accompanying; it follows the ALF and its final H then travels.

annotation.walkthrough: 'Dope' could be a drug or information; it is the informal word for a fool.
annotation.surface: Someone on drugs riding a bicycle beside a big woman.
annotation.definitionFit: Dope is slang for a stupid person, a plain synonym for this insult.

entries.clue: Movement for music and not for drama (9)

blocks.note: Kept as it is.
Anti = against, not for.
No (or Noh) is classical Japanese masked drama.

annotation.walkthrough: The clue seems to separate music from drama; 'and' is in fact the first piece of the answer, not a joining word.
annotation.surface: A choreographer's note: this movement is for the concert, not the stage play.
annotation.definitionFit: Italian tempo marks double as names for the movements played at them, and this one means a little quicker than andante.

entries.clue: According to recital, the Pobble does sugar! (7)

indicators.note: A recital is a speaking out loud, so we go by how the words sound, not how they are spelt.

blocks.note: Edward Lear's nonsense poem is The Pobble Who Has No Toes, so the Pobble lacks toes.

annotation.walkthrough: You need the Lear poem: the Pobble is a creature who lost his toes swimming the Bristol Channel.
annotation.surface: A nonsense-verse character caught in the act of eating sugar.
annotation.definitionFit: Milk sugar is the everyday name for it, so 'sugar' is the class the answer belongs to.

entries.clue: What ladies mark at ball includes both the last and the first dance (7)

indicators.note: CARDS takes both letters inside it, each in its own place.

blocks.note: At a ball a lady noted her partners on a dance card.
Z is the last letter of the alphabet.
A is the first letter.

annotation.walkthrough: The two letters do not go in together: Z sits after the C and A before the S. 'The last dance' looks like a phrase, but 'dance' stands alone as the definition.
annotation.surface: Ladies at a ball filling in their cards, with the final and opening dances both booked.
annotation.definitionFit: A Hungarian folk dance that speeds up from slow to wild, so 'dance' defines it by class.

entries.clue: Sweet / nothing (6)

blocks.note: In Britain a sweet is a dessert; think of one layered with sponge, custard and cream.
Nothing in the sense of a thing of no importance.

annotation.walkthrough: The slash splits the romantic phrase 'sweet nothing' into two separate definitions.
annotation.surface: A lover's sweet nothing whispered in an ear.
annotation.definitionFit: The same word is both a British layered pudding and a matter of no importance.

entries.clue: Stop circulating right-wing lie (4,5)

indicators.note: Something circulating goes round, so the front letter travels round to the back.

blocks.note: Stall = stop; circulating moves its S to the end.
A Tory is a British Conservative.

annotation.walkthrough: 'Stop circulating' reads as a plea to halt a rumour, which is why the surface is so smooth; the first word is the wordplay.
annotation.surface: A plea to stop spreading a false story put about by the political right.
annotation.definitionFit: An exaggerated, unbelievable tale is an idiom for a lie.

entries.clue: Terms at writing school may be stressed by them (7)

annotation.definition: Terms at writing school may be stressed by them

blocks.note: Reads as school terms at a college for writers; the setter means words, in the italic hand taught as a school of writing.
Reads as students feeling stress; the setter means words being emphasised.

annotation.walkthrough: Italic is a school of handwriting, and slanted type is how printed words are given stress.
annotation.surface: School terms spent learning to write can be stressful.
annotation.definitionFit: Printers emphasise terms by slanting them, so the clue describes the answer's use.

entries.clue: Way to eat Indian spinach dish (7)

indicators.note: To eat something is to take it inside you, so LANE swallows the other piece.

blocks.note: A lane is a way.
Sag (saag) is spinach in Indian cooking.

annotation.walkthrough: The surface asks how to eat an Indian dish, but 'Indian spinach dish' is not a phrase: 'dish' is the definition, and the answer is Italian.
annotation.surface: Advice on how best to eat an Indian spinach curry.
annotation.definitionFit: An Italian baked pasta, so 'dish' defines it by class.

entries.clue: Part of cathedral day out ends in panic and patriarch in flap (4,6)

indicators.note: A day out is a trip away, and letters out of place are rearranged.
The ends of words are their last letters.
The pieces sit in the flap, inside its letters.

blocks.note: A lapel is the flap on a coat front; its first letter opens the answer.
The letters of day, rearranged.
The last letter of panic.
The last letter of patriarch.
The rest of the lapel.

annotation.walkthrough: 'Ends in panic' reads as a story's outcome, but 'ends' belongs to both panic and patriarch, while 'in' is the container.
annotation.surface: A cathedral day trip ending in panic, with the patriarch in a flap.
annotation.definitionFit: A chapel dedicated to Our Lady, the Virgin Mary, usually behind a cathedral's high altar, so it is part of the building.

entries.clue: Too emotional, some cases (4)

indicators.note: To case something is to enclose it, so the words encase the answer.

blocks.note: Hidden across the end of emotional and the start of some.

annotation.walkthrough: 'Too emotional' reads as one phrase; 'Too' is the definition on its own.
annotation.surface: A verdict that some cases are handled too emotionally.
annotation.definitionFit: Both words mean 'in addition', a plain synonym.

entries.clue: Players indebted to closing season display (6-8)

indicators.note: Closing on something means shutting round it, so OWING closes round the next piece.

blocks.note: The wind are an orchestra's wind players.
Owing = in debt.
To dress a salad is to season it.

annotation.walkthrough: 'Closing season' looks like the end of a theatre run, but 'season' is the cook's verb and 'closing' the container.
annotation.surface: Performers in debt at the end of the season's show.
annotation.definitionFit: A shop's window display is literally this, and it also means a show put on to hide the truth.

entries.clue: Mo, I should add muscle (7)

blocks.note: A mo and a trice are both a moment.
A postscript is what a letter-writer adds at the end.

annotation.walkthrough: Mo is British slang for a moment, as in 'half a mo', not a name.
annotation.surface: Someone called Mo being told he should add some muscle.
annotation.definitionFit: The muscle at the back of the upper arm, so 'muscle' defines by class.

entries.clue: I’m on key with 3, doing puns outrageously (5,4)

indicators.note: Doing something outrageously means doing it wildly, out of all order, so the letters are scrambled.

blocks.note: The letters to rearrange.

annotation.walkthrough: On a British keyboard the £ symbol shares the 3 key, and the definition speaks as the symbol itself.
annotation.surface: Someone owning up to being keyed up and punning shamelessly.
annotation.definitionFit: The £ symbol describes itself: on a UK keyboard it sits on the key with 3.

entries.clue: I’ll ask you to raise your glasses to Daisy’s relative (7)

annotation.definition: I’ll ask you to raise your glasses

blocks.note: Kept as it is.
Asters belong to the daisy family.

annotation.walkthrough: Daisy looks like a person's name; it is the flower, and its relative is another flower.
annotation.surface: A toastmaster asking the room to drink to Daisy's family.
annotation.definitionFit: The definition is the speech of whoever proposes a toast, so it describes the answer in its own words.

entries.clue: I try this out on husband of a certain age (9)

indicators.note: A try-out is a test run, and letters worked out are rearranged.

blocks.note: The letters to rearrange.
H = husband.

annotation.walkthrough: 'Of a certain age' usually hints at middle age; here it is simply about one particular age.
annotation.surface: A woman trying a line on her middle-aged husband.
annotation.definitionFit: Being about thirty is being of a certain age, read literally.

entries.clue: Inordinately proud to leave school unqualified (4,3)

indicators.note: Inordinate means excessive, but it splits as in-ordinate, not in order, so the letters are shuffled.

blocks.note: The letters to rearrange.

annotation.walkthrough: 'Inordinately proud' reads as vanity; the 'to' is part of the letters, not a link.
annotation.surface: Someone too proud to stay on at school to get qualifications.
annotation.definitionFit: Quitting education before finishing is the idiom's meaning, so the definition paraphrases it.

entries.clue: Ridicule “100-year-old” bones (7)

blocks.note: To rib is to tease.
C = 100 in Roman numerals.
How many years old you are is your age.

annotation.walkthrough: The quotation marks bundle '100-year-old' as one mocking label; it splits into a numeral and a word.
annotation.surface: Mocking a centenarian's old bones.
annotation.definitionFit: The set of bones round the chest, so 'bones' describes it collectively.

entries.clue: Sooner make do with drop in energy (7)

indicators.note: Energy is E, and in a down answer a drop moves it lower, so the E slips one place down the word.

blocks.note: To do a play or a trick is to perform it.

annotation.walkthrough: 'Make do' reads as a phrase meaning to manage; it splits, with 'make' ending the definition and 'do' starting the wordplay.
annotation.surface: Advice to get by early on with less energy.
annotation.definitionFit: Pre- means before and to form is to make, so making something sooner is to preform it.

entries.clue: State I entered in treatment for my own good (7)

indicators.note: The letter enters, going in among the others.
Letters that get treatment are worked over and rearranged.

blocks.note: Letters to rearrange.
G = good, added to the letters to rearrange.
Kept as it is, going in near the end.

annotation.walkthrough: 'For my own good' sounds like a patient's grumble; 'good' is only a G.
annotation.surface: A patient insisting their treatment was for their own good.
annotation.definitionFit: One of the fifty US states, so 'State' defines by class.

entries.clue: Victoria’s one clip encapsulates beginning of loving marriage (7)

indicators.note: To encapsulate is to enclose in a capsule, so the clip holds the letter inside it.
The beginning of a word is its first letter.

blocks.note: Queen Victoria's royal 'we' ('We are not amused') stood for 'I', one.
To dock is to clip, as a tail.
First letter of loving.

annotation.walkthrough: 'Clip' looks like a hair clip or brooch; it is the verb to cut short.
annotation.surface: A hair clip of Queen Victoria's holding a memento of a loving marriage.
annotation.definitionFit: Wedlock is the formal word for the married state, a plain synonym.

entries.clue: Luxuriant new houseplant has irregularly shaped leaves (7)

indicators.note: Making something new remakes it, so the remaining letters are rearranged.
Irregularly means not in a regular run, so the letters of HAS are taken from scattered places.
Leaves is the verb, departs, so those letters go.

blocks.note: The word to take letters from.
H, A and S removed from houseplant.

annotation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' reads as foliage of the houseplant; it is the verb.
annotation.surface: A lush new houseplant whose leaves come in odd shapes.
annotation.definitionFit: Both words mean rich and lavish, a plain synonym.

entries.clue: Set about arranging letters in the grid (7)

indicators.note: Arranging the letters in something puts them in a new order.

blocks.note: The letters to rearrange.

annotation.walkthrough: 'Set about' reads as 'began', which suits a solver starting a crossword; here it means surrounded, as a girth goes round a horse.
annotation.surface: Instructions for starting to fill in a crossword grid.
annotation.definitionFit: To girth is to encircle, so girthed means set about in the sense of surrounded.

entries.clue: Routine studied in guest house, say (5-3-6)

indicators.note: One piece is in the other, sitting inside its letters.

blocks.note: A B and B (bed and breakfast) is a small guest house.
To read a subject is to study it at university.
To utter is to say.

annotation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like 'for example' after guest house; it is a verb giving the last piece.
annotation.surface: Someone describing their studies in a guest house.
annotation.definitionFit: Bread-and-butter work is the basic, everyday kind, an idiom for routine.

entries.clue: Putin’s agreed to render part of wall (4)

blocks.note: Da is Russian for yes.
To render a service is to do it.

annotation.walkthrough: 'Render' suggests plastering a wall, which fits the surface but here just means do.
annotation.surface: Putin agreeing to have part of a wall plastered.
annotation.definitionFit: The lower band of an interior wall, often panelled, so 'part of wall' defines it by location.

entries.clue: Bankrupt rogue hosts balls (10)

indicators.note: A host has guests inside the house, so one word holds the other.

blocks.note: Impish = roguish, mischievous, the adjective sense of rogue.
In cricket an over is a set of six balls.

annotation.walkthrough: 'Bankrupt rogue' reads as a broke scoundrel, but 'Bankrupt' is the verb, to ruin, and 'rogue' an adjective.
annotation.surface: A penniless scoundrel throwing parties.
annotation.definitionFit: To bankrupt someone is to make them poor, the verb sense of the definition.

entries.clue: Forget it — Ned’s no longer coming about pests (6)

indicators.note: Something no longer coming about has stopped surrounding, so the letters that went round the outside are dropped.

blocks.note: Never mind = forget it.
N, E and D removed: NE at the front and D at the back.

annotation.walkthrough: Ned is split around the answer, NE at the start and D at the end, which is what 'coming about' means.
annotation.surface: Giving up on Ned, who won't come round to deal with the pests any more.
annotation.definitionFit: Rats, mice and the like are pests, a plain synonym.

entries.clue: Drew small craft, back to front, alongside front of dock (8)

indicators.note: The back letter moves round to the front.
Alongside means placed next to, so the next letter is added on.
The front of a word is its first letter.

blocks.note: Ketches are small two-masted sailing boats; the final S moves to the front.
First letter of dock.

annotation.walkthrough: 'Craft' is plural here; 'Drew' looks like a name but is the past tense of draw.
annotation.surface: Boats being brought stern first to moor beside the dock.
annotation.definitionFit: To draw roughly is to sketch, so drew is a plain synonym in the past tense.
